findings.step: Multiply by the total usage of 500 billion litres:  [box expects: 100]
findings.why: The box has no unit label and the sentence never says the answer should be given 'in billions'. A student who correctly computes 0.2 x 500 = 100 has no cue that they should type '100' rather than the full number (100,000,000,000) or '100 billion' — this is the exact scale-ambiguity trap.
findings.fix: Label the box 'billion litres', or reword to 'Multiply 500 by your decimal (staying in billions of litres):'

findings.step: Check: agriculture in the same way, in billions of litres =  [box expects: 350]
findings.why: This is a dangling clause with no verb — 'agriculture in the same way, in billions of litres = ___' does not read as an instruction. The student must infer unaided that they should re-run the whole read-percentage -> decimal -> multiply-by-500 chain using agriculture's 70% share.
findings.fix: Reword to 'Check: repeat the same calculation for agriculture (70% of 500 billion litres), in billions of litres ='

findings.step: Check: the tertiary sector in the same way, in people =  [box expects: 15600]
findings.why: Same condensed-check pattern: no verb, and the student must both find tertiary's percentage on the chart (never given in the walk) and redo the decimal-and-multiply-by-24,000 method entirely unaided.
findings.fix: Reword to 'Check: read tertiary's percentage from the chart and repeat the calculation, in people ='

findings.step: Check: the angle for vans in the same way, in degrees =  [box expects: 60]
findings.why: Vans' count (120) is given in the question, but the instruction never says to use it — 'the angle for vans in the same way' assumes the student remembers to multiply 120 by the 0.5 degrees-per-vehicle figure from two steps earlier without being told to.
findings.fix: Reword to 'Check: multiply the 120 vans by your degrees-per-vehicle figure ='

findings.step: Check: the renewables angle to the nearest degree =  [box expects: 22]
findings.why: Renewables' percentage is never stated anywhere in the walk (only nuclear's 10% was given), so this compressed line silently requires the student to go back to the chart for a new figure AND redo the decimal/x360 method with no breakdown, unlike the scaffolded nuclear steps above it.
findings.fix: Reword to 'Check: read renewables' percentage from the chart, convert to a decimal and multiply by 360 ='

findings.step: Check: abrasion events worked the same way =  [box expects: 80]
findings.why: Abrasion's percentage (40%) is never given in the walk — the student must independently read it off the chart and redo the decimal-times-200 method, but 'worked the same way' is a passive fragment that doesn't say what to do.
findings.fix: Reword to 'Check: read abrasion's percentage from the chart and multiply by the 200 events ='

findings.step: Check: the 10-20 class worked the same way =  [box expects: 30]
findings.why: The 10-20 class's frequency density is never given in text — the student must read a new value off the histogram and multiply it by the class width themselves, but 'worked the same way' doesn't say to do either of those things.
findings.fix: Reword to 'Check: read the 10-20 class's density from the chart and multiply by its width ='

findings.step: Check: the fossil fuels angle to the nearest degree =  [box expects: 227]
findings.why: Fossil fuels' 63% is given in the question, so the data is available, but the line jumps straight to 'the angle' with no verb — it silently expects the student to redo the entire decimal/x360 chain unaided, right after that chain was broken into 3 separate steps for renewables.
findings.fix: Reword to 'Check: convert 63% to a decimal and multiply by 360 for fossil fuels ='

findings.step: Check: migrants from the EU and Other combined =  [box expects: 4400]
findings.why: EU (45%) and Other (10%) are both given in the question, but the phrase names only the answer, not the method — the student must independently remember to add the two percentages, convert to a decimal, and multiply by 8,000, exactly as was scaffolded in 3 separate steps for Asia+Africa above.
findings.fix: Reword to 'Check: add 45% and 10%, convert to a decimal, and multiply by 8,000 ='

findings.step: That share as a decimal:  [box expects: 0.2]
findings.why: Unlike bronze[1] in the same lesson, which spells out '(percentage divided by a hundred)', this step jumps straight to '20% -> 0.2' with no reminder of the method — exactly the kind of unexplained percent-to-decimal jump that trips a weaker reader.
findings.fix: Add the same parenthetical used in bronze[1]: 'That share as a decimal (percentage divided by a hundred):'

findings.step: That share as a decimal:  [box expects: 0.2]
findings.why: Same unexplained percent-to-decimal step as bronze[6]; by silver tier the method has likely been seen once already, so the risk is lower, but the walk still never restates it.
findings.fix: Add '(percentage divided by a hundred)' for consistency with bronze[1].

findings.step: That share as a decimal:  [box expects: 0.1]
findings.why: Repeats the unexplained percent-to-decimal jump seen elsewhere in this lesson.
findings.fix: Add '(percentage divided by a hundred)' as in bronze[1].

findings.step: That share as a decimal:  [box expects: 0.35]
findings.why: Same recurring gap — 35% to 0.35 is never explained in this problem.
findings.fix: Add '(percentage divided by a hundred)' as in bronze[1].

findings.step: That combined share as a decimal:  [box expects: 0.45]
findings.why: Same recurring gap at gold tier — 45% to 0.45 is never explained anywhere in the lesson text itself.
findings.fix: Add '(percentage divided by a hundred)' as in bronze[1].

findings.step: The 20-30 class: density multiplied by its width of 10 gives a frequency of  [box expects: 25]  /  The 30-50 class is 20 wide. Its frequency is  [box expects: 30]
findings.why: The final answer box is in 'people', but neither of these two frequency-density conversion steps is labelled, and 'frequency' is an unfamiliar term dressed up as a plain number here — a student could plausibly leave it as a bare density-derived figure without realising it now represents a headcount.
findings.fix: Label both boxes 'people' (e.g. 'gives a frequency of ___ people').

findings.step: Frequency of the 0-5mm class (density times its width):  [box expects: 20]  /  Frequency of the 5-20mm class:  [box expects: 30]
findings.why: Same frequency-density issue as gold[1]: the final answer is in 'pebbles' but these two conversion steps carry no unit, leaving the meaning of the raw number ambiguous mid-walk.
findings.fix: Label both boxes 'pebbles' (e.g. 'Frequency of the 0-5mm class... = ___ pebbles').

findings.step: the nearest point to the left is at a birth rate of 22, with infant mortality of  [box expects: 32]  /  the nearest point to the right is at a birth rate of 28, with infant mortality of  [box expects: 45]
findings.why: The question and every walk step give raw numbers like '32' and '45' for infant mortality with no unit anywhere in the visible text (only the main answer box metadata says 'per 1000') — a student reading just the walk could reasonably read these as percentages or raw counts rather than a rate per 1,000 births.
findings.fix: Add '(per 1000 births)' to at least the first reading, e.g. 'with infant mortality of ___ per 1000 births'.

findings.step: Check the spacing. Your estimate minus the 35 mm reading gives  [box expects: 2]
findings.why: 'The 35 mm reading' is shorthand for 'the discharge value at 35mm (16 cumecs)', but a struggling reader could easily substitute the literal '35' into the subtraction (18 - 35) instead of the discharge value 16, since the phrase names the axis position, not the quantity being subtracted.
findings.fix: Reword to 'Your estimate minus the discharge at 35 mm (16 cumecs) gives ___ cumecs' and label the box 'cumecs'.

findings.step: intro: A tight rising pattern plus one point far above it: an economy built on oil and gas with very few people to divide the emissions between produces exactly this outlier.
findings.why: This is one long run-on sentence with an embedded colon and the main verb ('produces') held back until the very end — a 15-year-old would likely need to re-read it to work out what is doing the 'producing'.
findings.fix: Split it: 'This is a tight rising pattern with one point far above it. That point is an economy built on oil and gas, with very few people to divide its emissions between — exactly the profile of this kind of outlier.'

findings.step: On the side axis, one gridline step is worth  [box expects: 10]
findings.why: The chart is in mm (established in the question) but this step's wording never repeats the unit, unlike the very next step which reads '...It reads 60 mm.' — a small inconsistency in an otherwise clear problem.
findings.fix: Label the box 'mm'.

findings.step: On the side axis, one labelled step is worth  [box expects: 5]
findings.why: Same gap as bronze[0]: the chart is in °C but this scale-reading step doesn't say so.
findings.fix: Label the box '°C'.

findings.step: One labelled step on the side axis is worth  [box expects: 5000]
findings.why: Population chart's gridline value is given with no unit; less risky than a true scale-conversion trap since the axis is already in raw people-counts, but still an unlabelled number sitting on its own.
findings.fix: Label the box 'people'.

findings.step: The whole 2020 bar reaches the  [box expects: 100 (unit label: ' level')]  /  Together they reach the  [box expects: 24 (unit label: ' level')]
findings.why: 'Reaches the 100 level' and 'reach the 24 level' are unusual phrasings for a percentage stacked bar — GCSE students are used to '100%' and '24%', not '100 level'.
findings.fix: Reword both to use % directly, e.g. 'The whole 2020 bar reaches ___%' and 'Together they reach ___%'.

findings.step: The death rate goes from 25 in 1960 to 12 in 1980, a fall of  [box expects: 13]  (and the birth-rate steps that follow)
findings.why: Birth and death rates are conventionally 'per 1000 population', but this problem never states a unit anywhere — neither in the question nor any walk step — for any of the raw numbers (25, 12, 45, 40, 24, 16). It doesn't block the multiple-choice answer, but leaves every figure in the walk unitless.
findings.fix: Add '(per 1000 population)' to the question stem or the first birth/death rate reading.

findings.step: 450 − 160 =  [box expects: 290 (unit label: ' thousand pounds of change')]
findings.why: The label 'thousand pounds of change' is wordier and less natural than the '£ ___ thousand' format used everywhere else in the same problem, and 'of change' is redundant once the subtraction is shown.
findings.fix: Shorten the label to 'thousand pounds' (or '£ thousand') to match the earlier steps.

findings.step: Over the same stretch visitors go from 200 to 800, a rise of  [box expects: 600]
findings.why: The paired step just above it ('a rise of 6 hours') is unit-labelled, but this visitor-count step isn't, which reads as an inconsistency even though 'visitors' is contextually obvious.
findings.fix: Label the box 'visitors' to match the parallel 'hours' label above it.

findings.step: The point furthest right, at 99% literacy, has a birth rate of  [box expects: 9]  (and 'At 70% literacy the birth rate is  [box expects: 25]')
findings.why: The very first reading in this problem says 'Its birth rate per 1000 is 42', establishing the unit, but the next two birth-rate readings drop 'per 1000' entirely — a minor inconsistency that could leave a student unsure whether later numbers are the same measure.
findings.fix: Repeat 'per 1000' in the later steps too, e.g. 'has a birth rate per 1000 of ___'.
